analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve every major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill requiring a congressional vote on every major federal rule has sat untouched in a Senate committee since February 2025, backed by 23 of 53 Republican senators and no Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require both houses of Congress and the president to approve every major federal rule — those with $100 million or more in annual economic effects — before it takes effect, and any rule Congress fails to approve within 70 days dies. Rules already in force would expire after 10 years, and each year agencies would have to put up at least 10% of their major rules for a congressional vote, with unapproved rules ceasing to apply. Deregulatory actions would be exempt from all of this, and a regulatory budget would cap the net cost of new rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Large regulated companies — fossil fuel and chemical producers, banks, drug and device makers, food processors, and their trade groups — would gain a practical veto over federal regulation. Nothing costing $100 million a year or more could take effect unless both chambers pass and the president signs a resolution, so one chamber's inaction kills any major rule. Companies could also watch existing rules expire, challenge in court whether a rule is truly "major," and claim an affirmative defense if a statute did not clearly forbid their conduct.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large regulated industries and trade groups

how_it_helps.text: Major rules — those with $100 million or more in annual economic effects, major cost or price increases, or significant effects on competition or jobs — take effect only if Congress enacts a resolution of approval; if none is enacted within 70 days, the rule is deemed not approved and never takes effect, meaning a single chamber's inaction can kill any big rule.

The approval requirement is one-sided: rules identified as deregulatory actions are exempt from the approval process entirely, so repealing protections stays easy while issuing them becomes nearly impossible, and an OMB 'regulatory budget' caps net new regulatory costs at zero unless the OMB director sets a higher allowance.

Existing major rules expire 10 years after approval, agencies must annually designate at least 10% of their in-effect major rules for a congressional vote with unapproved rules losing effect, and companies gain a court challenge to invalidate rules a judge decides should have been classified as major — giving regulated parties ways to unwind rules already in force.

Significant agency guidance documents — like FDA or SEC interpretive advice — would be treated as rules, and significant guidance as major rules, slowing down the informal channels agencies use, while defendants gain an affirmative defense whenever their conduct was not clearly forbidden by the underlying statute.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal protections — clean air and water, safe food and drugs, safe workplaces, honest financial markets, consumer financial safeguards — would bear the cost. Any major protection defaults to not happening when Congress does not act, existing protections lapse after 10 years unless Congress affirmatively renews each one, and even a president's emergency exception covers a rule for only 90 days.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, workers, and communities relying on federal safeguards

drawbacks.text: Because 'no rule' is the default, public protections — pollution limits, workplace safety standards, food and drug safety, consumer financial rules — would be blocked whenever Congress fails to vote, and rules already in effect would expire after 10 years unless each is individually renewed; even emergency health-and-safety rules get only one 90-day window without a new law.

The procedural design is asymmetric by intent: approval resolutions cannot be amended, committees are automatically discharged with a mandated floor vote, and the Senate path bypasses normal debate limits — all to ease passage of deregulation while deregulatory actions skip the approval process altogether, so gridlock systematically produces fewer protections.

The bill is selective about whose rules it restrains: monetary policy by the Federal Reserve is exempt, and rules under the Telecommunications Act of 1996 are carved out of the major-rule category, so those industries keep an easier path than everyone else.

An honest supporter would have to concede that the bill would also hobble an administration of its own party — any future Congress, narrowly divided, could rarely muster the votes to approve even wanted rules, making agencies nearly unable to act on problems Congress itself has ordered them to address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim — forcing Congress to own the rules it delegates to agencies — is a genuine constitutional argument, and its transparency pieces (posting all agency guidance online, a one-time GAO cost study) cost the public little. But the core mechanism makes "no protection" the default: a special interest only needs to keep one chamber from voting to kill any major rule, while repeal of protections requires nothing and new regulatory costs face a hard budget cap. The accountability gains are diffuse and uncertain; the costs land directly on people who depend on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial safeguards. As written, the cost to the public clearly outweighs the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security Committee in February 2025 and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the bill on February 6, 2025, joined by 23 Republican cosponsors — 23 of the Senate's 53 Republicans; no Democrat has signed on.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs — the committee whose chairman is the bill's own sponsor, Senator Paul.
Since that referral, the committee has taken no action: no hearings, no markup, no vote appear anywhere in the bill's action history.
The current Congress runs through January 2027, so the bill technically remains alive, but nothing in the record suggests movement toward a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody yet. Current law still lets agencies issue major rules without a congressional veto, so the industries the bill would help have gained nothing, while the public has not yet lost anything either — the bill is simply parked, and could still move before the Congress ends.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; existing rules still apply

sides.party_line_note: All 24 sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans — 23 of the Senate's 53 Republicans plus the sponsor — with zero Democrats, and there has been no vote to reveal any cross-party support.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel, chemical, and heavy manufacturers
industries.note: Environmental and safety rules on pollution, emissions, and workplace hazards almost always exceed the $100 million major-rule threshold, so the bill hands these companies a veto: one chamber's inaction kills the rule, deregulatory repeals face no such hurdle, and existing protections expire after 10 years.

Financial rules from the SEC, CFPB, and banking agencies routinely cost over $100 million and would need congressional approval, while an affirmative defense and private right of action give firms tools to delay or void rules in court.

FDA safety rules and much of its informal guidance would be classified as rules or major rules needing congressional approval, slowing safety requirements and giving companies litigation leverage over the agency.
The bill explicitly excludes rules under the Telecommunications Act of 1996 from the major-rule category, so FCC consumer and competition rules keep an easier path than rules on every other industry.

analysis.trajectory: Very likely to die quietly. REINS-style bills have passed the House in earlier Congresses but never cleared the Senate; this version has only 23 of 53 Republicans behind it and no Democrats, far short of the 60 votes needed to break a filibuster, and the committee chaired by its own sponsor has scheduled nothing in the months since referral. Expect it to sit until this Congress ends in January 2027.
